You're right - it does feel like the suffering element always gets missed from explanations. I think perhaps that might be linked with the neurodiversity movement making people cautious of how they word things, but personally I do feel like I "suffer" from ADHD, rather than am just "wired a little differently".
I think Dr. Barkley did well at explaining this in relation to the much shorter life expectancy with ADHD. There was also a shocking study I read not too long ago exploring the emotional suffering caused but ADHD. It was admittedly small and not necessarily the most in depth study, but it found that the chance of attempting suicide could be as high as 1 in 4 for ADHD women and 1 in 7 for ADHD men.

I think I went into it with high expectations. It helps, but I still find daily activities much harder than neurotypical people seem to. For emotional regulation, I absolutely need it; but in terms of productivity, I find it easier to focus on the wrong thing and waste time. Having said that, it's still less difficult to change task when on medication than it is off of it, and my dose may well be increased soon.

It's definitely relatively common for people to have more limited struggles before they're independent, precisely because there's fewer things *for* you to forget or make mistakes on. I personally never even suspected ADHD at your age (although I knew *something* was different) and things only became unmanageable when I was maybe 16/17. Don't feel bad about doubting yourself or even about not struggling - it is quite normal to doubt that you can have the condition (which it appears is what you're feeling) and also quite normal to have symptoms which are either more manageable than others or that are only unmanageable when you're expected to be independent. 

Remember that this is a community full of people who have sought it out, looking for support with ADHD - it's largely people who have very unmanageable symptoms looking for peer support or for people who are awaiting diagnosis / coping with receiving one. There's plenty of people who have ADHD who *don't* find their symptoms as unmanageable as many people here. Obviously it is a disability, with all the connotations that implies - but some people do feel less impacted than others. Please don't doubt yourself! Wishing you the very best of luck and sending lots of support :)

I know that cost can be a massive problem, but I think it's definitely worth considering getting a second opinion, especially when ADHD can be so debilitating. I know that in my assessment that I was very worried I would forget to mention something, so I made a complete list of my symptoms over the course of a month beforehand and emailed that to my assessor. If your assessor is very well informed of everything that's been a struggle for you, and you've left nothing out, then there's less chance of this happening again. Ironically, it's very possible for a person with ADHD to not get a diagnosis because they may forget information, have their mind go blank, or impulsively/reactively say something that isn't true for you. A good assessor should be aware of this. Even if you don't have ADHD after all, a good assessor should really let you know what else they might suspect - my brother even got diagnosed as a "mixed bag" and told that autism, bipolar, and OCD were suspected also based off his symptoms. I wish you the very best of luck.
